name: Boldenone

card.summary: A horse steroid used by bodybuilders for slow, steady gains; no human trials exist.
card.note: Veterinary drug; not approved for humans; prohibited in sport; animal studies report organ toxicity.

quick.overview:
Boldenone is an injectable anabolic steroid, best known as Equipoise, a veterinary drug for horses. Bodybuilders use it illicitly for steady muscle gain.

No human trials of boldenone were found. Claims about its effects on appearance rest on user reports and a single encyclopedic overview.
quick.mechanism: It is a testosterone analogue that activates the androgen receptor and is reported to boost red blood cell production. Its long-acting ester releases slowly after injection.
quick.risks: Animal studies report reproductive, liver, kidney and immune effects. It is not approved for humans in the US and is prohibited in sport.

lead: Boldenone is an anabolic-androgenic steroid (AAS) and a close chemical relative of testosterone, differing by one extra double bond in the A ring. In bodybuilding circles it is known by the name of its long-acting veterinary form, boldenone undecylenate, sold for horses as Equipoise or "EQ". People who use it illicitly do so in pursuit of a fuller, more muscular physique, and talk about it as a steady, slow-building anabolic with an appetite boost.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes boldenone as mainly anabolic with low androgenic potency; like other AAS it activates the androgen receptor, increases nitrogen retention and protein synthesis, raises appetite and stimulates release of erythropoietin in the kidneys.[1] The chain people point to is more protein synthesis and appetite, then more training capacity and mass, then a bigger, leaner-looking physique.

Boldenone has never been marketed as a human medicine under its own name. Ciba reportedly patented it in 1949, and the undecylenate ester was sold for humans as Parenabol in the late 1960s and early 1970s before being discontinued; Squibb later introduced it as the veterinary product Equipoise.[1] No human clinical trial of boldenone for muscle or appearance is known, it is a controlled substance in several countries, and it is prohibited under anti-doping rules.[1][2]

It is discussed mostly on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where posters treat it as a slow, supporting compound in stacks and argue over how it compares with testosterone and whether it aromatises.[3][4][5] Research that does exist is mainly veterinary or in laboratory animals, including rat studies that report testicular and hepatorenal changes and a broiler study that reported blood and tissue changes.[10][11]

chain: Androgen receptor activation and appetite increase
More protein synthesis and nitrogen retention
More muscle mass and a fuller physique
angle.text: Users describe boldenone as a slow, steady builder of lean mass, with appetite and endurance benefits that support heavier training. These effects are reported by users and described in pharmacology summaries; they have not been measured in human trials.

paras: In veterinary medicine boldenone undecylenate is given by intramuscular injection to horses to improve body weight, muscular strength and red blood cell production during debilitation from illness or surgery.[2] A broiler study notes that the product was sold for cattle and veal calves and approved by the US FDA for horses, and that most countries prohibit its use in meat production; the authors also describe EU bans on hormone use in food-producing animals.[11] Some farm use as an illegal growth promoter is described in the toxicology literature.[10]

It is not approved for human therapeutic use in the United States, and in Ukraine a product named Boldenol is reported to be marketed for human consumption.[1][2] Illicit users in bodybuilding take it for muscle gain and endurance, with the slow-release ester valued for steady effects.[2] A rat toxicology paper describes bodybuilders and athletes as using it to build muscle and improve performance by promoting protein synthesis, and says users often exceed recommended veterinary doses, in some cases by more than a hundredfold, for competitive or aesthetic reasons.[10]

Forum users describe it as a companion to testosterone or other compounds rather than a stand-alone choice.[3][6] Wikipedia lists veterinary brand names Boldebal H, Equipoise and Sybolin, and a veterinary combination with methandriol sold as Drive.[1] Because it is not a human medicine in most countries, people who use it for physique purposes obtain it outside medical channels; this article does not cover sourcing or administration.

Boldenone (code RU-18761, also called delta-1-testosterone or 1-dehydrotestosterone, systematic name androsta-1,4-dien-17-beta-ol-3-one) is testosterone with an extra double bond between carbons 1 and 2; its formula is C19H26O2 and a related compound is quinbolone, its 17-cyclopentenyl enol ether.[1] Like other anabolic-androgenic steroids it is an agonist of the androgen receptor. Wikipedia describes its activity as mainly anabolic with low androgenic potency, increasing nitrogen retention, protein synthesis and appetite and stimulating erythropoietin release in the kidneys.[1] Boldenone itself has never been marketed; the pharmaceutical form is the undecylenate ester, whose elimination half-life after intramuscular injection is about 14 days.[1]

An AI-generated encyclopedic overview, treated here with caution, reports a higher anabolic-to-androgenic ratio than testosterone, slow release of the ester over weeks, and increased red blood cell production in equine trials.[2] Human pharmacokinetic information comes mostly from non-medical use rather than trials.[2] Wikipedia's page lists pregnancy category X in the US and Australia.[1]

Boldenone also occurs naturally at trace levels. Wikipedia reports it in the scent gland of the aquatic beetle Ilybius fenestratus and notes that, in calves never given the drug, urinary 17-alpha-boldenone tracks the phytosterol content of the diet, at levels below doping attention limits.[1] The AI-generated overview links some positive doping tests to contaminated meat.[2]

A study of broiler chicks describes how illegal use in food animals is detected: laboratories look for 17-beta or 17-alpha boldenone in edible tissue, hair, faeces or urine, the main cattle metabolite is 17-alpha-boldenone, and because boldenone can also form from phytosterols in vegetable fat, a positive result does not always show illegal treatment.[11]

Ciba reportedly patented boldenone in 1949 and developed several experimental esters in the 1950s and 1960s. Boldenone undecylenate was introduced for clinical use as Parenabol, saw some use in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and was discontinued before the end of the 1970s. Squibb later introduced it for veterinary use as Equipoise, most commonly in horses.[1] In Ukraine a product named Boldenol is marketed for human consumption.[1]

Its bodybuilding reputation grew from the veterinary product: the abbreviation EQ and the product name Equipoise are how it is usually referred to in forum threads.[3][8] Anabolic steroids as a class date to the 1930s, when testosterone was discovered and synthesised, and an estimated one to three million people in the United States are thought to have used AAS.[12]

Wikipedia lists boldenone as controlled in Brazil (Class C5), Canada (Schedule IV) and the United States (Schedule III), and prescription-only in the United Kingdom.[1] It appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency list of prohibited anabolic agents; the AI-generated overview reports it in roughly 5 percent of global anabolic steroid doping violations, while Wikipedia notes many cases among professional athletes.[1][2]

Wikipedia's boldenone page has no side-effect content and refers readers to the general anabolic steroid article.[1] That article lists adverse effects of AAS as a class: lipid changes, left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertension and arrhythmia; liver damage mostly associated with 17-alpha-alkylated oral steroids; suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis with testicular atrophy and reduced sperm production; acne, oily skin, body hair growth and androgenic alopecia; and psychiatric effects including aggression and dependence in some long-term users.[12] Boldenone undecylenate is an injectable ester rather than an oral alkylated compound, which bears on which of these class effects apply.

Laboratory studies in animals describe harms. In a study of 40 adult male Wistar rats given the undecylenate weekly for eight weeks, the authors reported reduced testis-to-body weight ratio, lower sperm count and motility, about 41 percent abnormal sperm versus about 17 percent in controls, falls in testicular testosterone, LH, FSH and estradiol, tubular degeneration and germ cell loss, and fewer androgen receptor-positive Sertoli and Leydig cells; co-treatment with vitamin C eased the oxidative and sperm changes but not the hormonal ones.[10] In 24 broiler chicks given a single injection, the authors reported higher red cell counts, higher liver and kidney enzyme markers, mild liver and kidney histological changes and altered meat pH and microbial counts, and described the results as preliminary because of the single dose and small groups.[11] The AI-generated overview summarises animal work describing reproductive, liver, kidney and immune effects.[2]

No human trial of boldenone safety was found. Forum posters describe their own experiences, such as worries about aromatisation and estrogen-related effects, and some describe it as gentler than other injectables.[3][4][5]

On T Nation, boldenone appears in discussions of testosterone-based stacks. Posters debate whether it aromatises and whether any aromatase-inhibiting effect of its metabolites could offset estrogen from other agents; one replies that any such effect would be too small against the aromatisation from large testosterone doses.[3] A post links to video discussions of whether boldenone aromatises into estradiol or acts as an aromatase inhibitor.[7] Another poster says boldenone did not blunt orgasm the way trenbolone or nandrolone can for him and suggests it for people who feel estrogenic and cannot lean out.[5]

Others mention its reported increase in endurance and tendon strength, and one poster credits an equipoise-plus-testosterone course for relief of joint pain and fatigue that lasted for weeks.[6][9] A poster describes experimenting with it as a testosterone substitute, noting they had heard it is considerably less potent than testosterone milligram for milligram.[8] Another lists boldenone among the few compounds they have tried and says some of what they read about these drugs is frightening.[13]

No studies found of boldenone in human clinical trials for muscle or appearance. Reported research is veterinary and animal, including equine pharmacokinetic work and rat and broiler toxicity studies.[2][10][11]

timeline.event: Testosterone is discovered and synthesised, opening the class of anabolic-androgenic steroids.[12]
Several experimental boldenone esters are developed.[1]
Boldenone undecylenate sold for human use as Parenabol; discontinued before the end of the 1970s.[1]
Squibb introduces boldenone undecylenate for veterinary use as Equipoise.[1]
Study of veal calves reports that urinary 17-alpha-boldenone tracks dietary phytosterols in untreated animals.[1]

lore.intro: On T Nation, boldenone is discussed as a slow, mild component of stacks, valued for appetite and a lean look, with ongoing argument about its estrogen behaviour.[3][4]

claims.claim: EQ builds steady lean mass without the water-retention of some other compounds.
claims.believers: A poster describes using boldenone at low doses alongside testosterone because it did not dull orgasm the way trenbolone or nandrolone can for them, and suggests it for users who are estrogenic and struggle to lean out.[5]
claims.experts: No human trial has compared boldenone with other anabolics on body composition. Wikipedia describes it as mainly anabolic with low androgenic potency.[1]

claims.claim: Boldenone adds endurance and tendon strength.
claims.believers: A poster planning a multi-compound cycle says they considered boldenone for its reported increase in endurance and tendon strength.[6]
claims.experts: Boldenone is reported to stimulate erythropoietin, which relates to red blood cell production, and veterinary use targets horses' stamina and blood counts; no study of tendon effects in humans was found.[1][2]

claims.claim: Boldenone metabolites can offset estrogen from other compounds.
claims.believers: Some forum users argue boldenone acts as an aromatase inhibitor or does not aromatise much; others reply that any such effect would be too small to counter the aromatisation from large testosterone doses.[3][7]
claims.experts: The question of aromatase activity is not addressed in the general references consulted; no human trial addresses it.

claims.claim: Boldenone can replace testosterone in a trial run.
claims.believers: A poster describes experimenting with EQ as a TRT substitute, noting they had heard it is considerably less potent than testosterone milligram for milligram.[8]
claims.experts: Boldenone has never been marketed as a human therapy; the human product Parenabol was discontinued in the 1970s.[1]

claims.claim: Equipoise relieves joint pain and fatigue.
claims.believers: A poster credits an equipoise-plus-testosterone course with relief of joint pain and fatigue that lasted for weeks after stopping.[9]
claims.experts: No published human study has examined boldenone for joint pain or fatigue.

claims.claim: It is safe because it is mild.
claims.believers: Users commonly describe it as gentler than other injectables.[4][5]
claims.experts: Rat and broiler studies report reproductive, hepatorenal and haematological changes, and AAS as a class are associated with documented adverse effects; boldenone is prohibited in sport.[2][10][11][12]
